They agreed that they did. Then Tom asked whether they were going to pay him anything, and A.A. — young, frightened, and very sure of itself — said no, because "that would make you a professional. This is Alcoholics Anonymous. We must not mix money with spirituality." Tom's reply is one of the most useful sentences in our literature: "no money, no work. There it is — the whole Tradition, from a man with a broom, years before anyone wrote it down. He would carry the message for nothing, forever. He would not sweep the floor for nothing. a4744989eadf: August 15 — "A Billing Code." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. There is now a version of the conversation that is being invoiced. No
fd4cbeba0811: There is now a version of the conversation that is being invoiced. Not inside A.A. — outside it, where the hour a sober alcoholic spends with a struggling alcoholic is given a code and a rate, so that somewhere a third party can be billed for it. Watch what the mechanism does, because it needs no villain. The moment the hour is billable, the payer needs to know what happened in it, so the hour acquires paperwork. The paperwork needs goals, so the hour acquires a curriculum. The rate needs justifying, so the hour acquires outcomes — and the outcomes belong to whoever pays, which is never the drunk. Nothing about the two people in the room has changed, and everything about the hour has: it answers upward now. A.A. put its refusal of all this into one line of P-43, its pamphlet on the Traditions: "The meaning of Twelfth Step work cannot be measured in money" — because what actually changes hands in that hour is "of far greater worth — our very lives." A price does not simply pay for the hour. It measures it, and a measured hour ends up serving whoever holds the ruler. The free hour serves the man who needs it, because it cannot serve anything else.

11413777debd: August 16 — "Members Sold It First." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. The first people to sell recovery with A.A.'s name on it were
901ac84aae9a: The first people to sell recovery with A.A.'s name on it were A.A. members. That is not an outside accusation; it is the Fellowship's own record of the years after the Saturday Evening Post article of March 1941 made it famous. Membership jumped by thousands within the year, and the pins on the office wall map showed scores of new groups a week — most with no experienced member in them, nothing to steer by but the book and the mail. Into that vacuum came trouble: committees quarreled, orators held forth, groups split wide open, whole groups got drunk. And then the worst of it — Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age) that some members turned professional, "selling A.A. therapy for money to new prospects." His summary of the era: "Such was the beginning of a truly frightening experience that lasted a long time." Hold on to what that means. The threat this Tradition answers was never an invading industry; in 1941 there was no recovery industry to invade. The discovery was simpler and worse: when A.A. spreads faster than its principles, somebody inside will try to sell it — before any outsider ever does. The Tradition is not a wall built against outsiders. It is a mirror, written by people who had watched themselves.

a7c66bc87e8f: The message that reached us was free. Nobody billed us for the conversation that saved our lives — and that is not a small detail; it is why we could trust it. edda06c852da: August 19 — "It Was Never Complicated." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Tradition 8 says A.A. stays "forever nonprofessional" (Big
37958d63b6b4: Tradition 8 says A.A. stays "forever nonprofessional" (Big Book, p. 561). Two words, and both mean exactly what they mean everywhere else. Nonprofessional: not a job. Forever: not until the field matures, not until licensing improves, not until somebody builds a respectful business model. Forever. a210879feaef: The Night They Told Him No
3fe7ed173cec: It is 1937. Bill is broke, Lois is working at the department store, and their house on Clinton Street is full of drunks who are not paying board. Charlie Towns — who owns the hospital where Bill got sober — calls him in and makes him an offer: "I'll give you an office, a decent drawing account, and a very healthy slice of the profits. What I propose is perfectly ethical." Then the closer: "You can become a lay therapist, and more successful than anybody in the business." Bill never pretended he was above it: "There was nothing wrong whatever with becoming a lay therapist." He thought of Lois. He thought of his creditors. On the subway home a verse arrived like guidance — "The laborer is worthy of his hire" — and his mind was made up. Then he told the group. They sat there. Then one of them found his footing: "You tell us that Charlie's proposal is ethical. Sure, it's ethical. But what we've got won't run on ethics only; it has to be better." And finally: "This is a matter of life and death, Bill, and nothing but the very best will do." Someone reminded him of his own line — "sometimes the good is the enemy of the best." Bill wrote afterward that the members deciding together had outranked his own guidance: "Thus spoke the group conscience. The group was right and I was wrong; the voice on the subway was not the voice of God." The office was never rented. Tradition 8 is not an idea somebody had. It is the scar from that living room.
a698c01caa2d: The offer was ethical, and the group told him ethical was not the bar. When has the good thing been the enemy of the best thing, in my life?

6384100a9e4c: A.A. looked at owning treatment beds and refused, in writing. And hold on to this rule, because it works in every country and under every system: if someone is being paid, then someone is paying. The drunk, his family, an insurer, or every taxpayer at once — even when nobody sees a bill, recovery money is buying what A.A. gives away. So the man discharged after thirty days has learned the price of a meeting, and it is not a dollar. He was sold a free thing. A.A. never saw a cent, and never wanted one.

12dcf226cf53: November 1 — "The Credit." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. May 1940. The catcher for
7236d4f35e9c: May 1940. The catcher for the Cleveland Indians had just caught a no-hit game pitched by Bob Feller, and Rollie H. told the papers he had been sober in A.A. for a year. Before you decide what you think of him, take the reason. His drinking had been public knowledge, and when the story of his recovery broke, the credit went to the Oxford Group — he had stayed on with them after the Akron members left. Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers records what happened: "At that time, however, Rollie broke his silence and said no, the credit for his sobriety belonged to Alcoholics Anonymous." He did not do it for attention. He did it to correct a record that had A.A.'s work under somebody else's name. And it worked, exactly as he hoped. Bill W. wrote later (Pass It On) that "it did us plenty of good, temporarily, because alcoholics flocked in." Hundreds of them. It was also the first anonymity break the Fellowship had ever had at the national level, and A.A. has been arguing with itself about that week ever since.
93d3eabee01c: A man broke his anonymity to give A.A. credit it was being denied, hundreds of alcoholics came in because of it, and it was still the break that started everything. When has the generous thing I did spent something that wasn't mine to spend?
612f70e3ff00: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (Rollie H., May 1940); Pass It On.

7752d97347e5: November 10 — "Filmed Beside It." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Nobody has to claim
38c09ec7a142: Nobody has to claim an endorsement to collect one. The mechanism is proximity, and it is almost impossible to object to. A film crew shoots outside the building where the meeting is held. A promotional video is recorded in the hall an hour before the chairs go out. A photograph is taken at the door, with the sign in shot. No word is spoken about A.A. and none needs to be — the viewer supplies the connection, which is the entire reason the location was chosen. What has happened is that an outside body has borrowed the visual credibility of a Fellowship that has no mechanism for lending it and no committee that could have refused. The long form's phrase (Big Book, p. 565) is "Our relations with the general public should be characterized by personal anonymity," and the difficulty here is that nothing personal was broken. A building was filmed. But the building is where the anonymity lives, and after that footage runs, everyone who walks in has been seen walking in.
7f7a83bcb06e: No one claimed anything and no name was given — a building was filmed, and afterwards everyone who walks in has been seen walking in. What have I been associated with purely by standing near it?

4965a00843f8: Carried Away With the Desire to Serve
b8f50bb058af: October 1939. There was no Tradition Eleven — there were no Traditions at all — and a man in Detroit who had never made a speech in his life got himself onto the radio. A.A.'s history of its co-founder sets down the date (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "In October 1939, Archie managed to get a six-minute radio interview about his recovery in A.A. It was heard in a number of Midwest cities and certainly represented a first for the area." His own account sits in the Big Book (p. 254), and the phrase he chose for himself years afterward is the one to keep. "I, carried away with the desire to serve A.A., gave what was probably one of the first radio broadcasts about A.A., living through a case of mike fright and feeling like a million dollars when it was all over." Carried away with the desire to serve. He is not confessing to vanity and there is no sign of any — he was frightened, he did it anyway, and it helped. But notice what he could not possibly have had: any way of knowing where that ends. Nobody had it yet. This Tradition exists because a great many people just like Archie were each, individually, right.
9ca26506a776: A frightened man got himself on the radio out of nothing but a desire to help, and there was no way yet for anyone to know where it led. What am I doing for good reasons whose cost nobody has worked out yet?
8af1660836eb: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (October 1939); Big Book p. 254 ("The Man Who Mastered Fear").

8402b59e14d3: November 12 — "There Was No Dr. Armstrong." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. On 1 Marc
d4065820677a: On 1 March 1941 the <0>Saturday Evening Post</0> ran Jack Alexander's article, and A.A. was never small again (Big Book, p. xviii) — "By March 1941 the membership had shot up to 2,000," and within the year it was four times that. Read the article and you meet a physician (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) who is "still struggling to patch up his practice. The going is hard. He is in debt because of his contributions to the movement and the time he devotes gratis to alcoholics." The book calls him Dr. Armstrong. There was no Dr. Armstrong. It was Dr. Bob, printed under a false name to protect his own — the co-founder of A.A. appearing in the most important article ever written about it as somebody else entirely. Later, when a second Alexander piece was being prepared, Sister Ignatia asked Bill to keep her name out of that one. She was not a member; she was the nun who had admitted alcoholics to St. Thomas Hospital when nobody else would. Bill's answer drew the line exactly where the Tradition draws it. "To be anonymous, Sister, you'll have to take a little drink."
56b0bea57996: A.A.'s co-founder let himself be printed as a stranger so that the rule he asked others to keep would hold for him first. What would I give up to keep a rule I have asked other people to follow?
5bc7e457d8a5: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the Post article; Sister Ignatia); Big Book p. xviii.

f2543cc693d8: Not in the Meaning of This Tradition
9b6a30e316a6: This is the line the internet gets wrong more often than any other, and getting it wrong costs people at the margin. A.A.'s own literature, plainly (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "When people are asked what led them to seek A.A. help, the answer given most often is: "An A.A. member." Their chances would have been slim if all of us had remained completely in hiding. But many of us have chosen to tell our friends, neighbors, employers, co-workers, doctors, or spiritual advisers that we are in A.A. — and when we do so, we are not breaking our anonymity in the meaning of this Tradition." We are not breaking our anonymity. Telling your doctor is not a break. Telling your employer is not a break. Telling the man at work whose hands shake at nine in the morning is the single most effective thing anyone has ever done for this Fellowship, and it is precisely what the Tradition was built to keep possible. The level named is press, radio and films. Not the kitchen. Not the ward. Not the front seat of a car in a parking lot at four in the afternoon.
fd63d84d8e80: Telling one person face to face is not a break — it is what most members say brought them in. Who is the one person I could say it to quietly, with no camera anywhere near it?
32bdd80442ee: Grounded in: P-43 (Tradition Eleven); long form, Tradition 11.

6b4f62508c19: November 14 — "A Stranger on a Deadline." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A reporter
efa09c368c89: A reporter rings the number on the intergroup site, because the paper is running something about the new detox unit and wants a line from A.A. The GSR takes it, since she is the one who answers that phone. She is careful. She says she can't speak for A.A. as a whole. She gives the meeting times, explains what the Fellowship does and does not do, and gives her name the way she gives it in the rooms — first name, last initial. The reporter is decent and barely interested in her. But a copy editor at ten at night has a house style, the paper does not print initials, and her surname is in the phone book. It runs on page five beneath the words Alcoholics Anonymous. She did everything right except the one thing nobody had told her: the decision about how her name appeared was never hers to make. A.A. put it as sharply as it can be put (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) — an A.A. "who permits his name to appear in the press in connection with matters pertaining to A.A." has broken this Tradition. Permits. Nobody asked her.
